claims.text: The as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEA has an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited alloy has a relatively smooth surface.
The as-deposited alloy exhibits a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
Controlled argon plasma etching can increase surface roughness without altering the alloy's bulk composition or phase.
Low- to moderate-power plasma etching for short durations can preserve the alloy's mechanical stability.
Increasing surface roughness increases the density of surface nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transition.
A higher density of surface nucleation sites makes initiation of the magnetostructural transition more spatially homogeneous.
Surface irregularities lower local activation barriers for the alloy's phase transformation.
Lower local transformation barriers produce a smoother and more spatially distributed transition from the hexagonal state.
A smoother, spatially distributed first-order transition reduces transition sharpness and hysteresis.
The surface modification increases effective surface area and thereby enhances heat exchange during magnetic-cooling cycles.
Plasma-etched samples will exhibit a more gradual magnetocaloric transition than untreated as-deposited samples.
Plasma-etched samples will exhibit less hysteresis than untreated as-deposited samples under low applied fields.
Plasma etching will produce a smoother entropy-change profile.
Plasma etching will maintain or improve effective cooling performance under low-applied-field conditions.
The untreated baseline has a low surface-to-volume ratio that limits its heat-exchange rate.
The predictions are limited to single-phase hexagonal FeMnNiGeSi-type HEAs for which etching changes only surface topography and preserves bulk composition, phase, and mechanical integrity.
